difficultyRationale: Platform-estimated: EASY — a single concept (dimension equals the number of free coefficients left after independent homogeneous linear conditions) with a one-line count; about 1 minute for a prepared student.
concept: Dimension of a polynomial vector space cut out by homogeneous linear conditions on the coefficients.
stem:
Let $\mathcal{P}_6$ denote the real vector space of all polynomials in $x$ with real coefficients and degree at most $6$ (together with the zero polynomial), under the usual addition and scalar multiplication. Consider

$$
V = \{\, p \in \mathcal{P}_6 \;:\; p(-x) = p(x) \text{ for all } x \in \mathbb{R}, \text{ and } p(1) = 0 \,\}.
$$

$V$ is a subspace of $\mathcal{P}_6$. The dimension of $V$ is ________.

solution.quick:
Even polynomials in $\mathcal{P}_6$ have the form $a_0 + a_2x^2 + a_4x^4 + a_6x^6$ (4 free coefficients). The condition $p(1) = 0$ adds one more independent equation, $a_0 + a_2 + a_4 + a_6 = 0$, leaving $4 - 1 = 3$ free coefficients.
A basis is $\{x^2 - 1,\ x^4 - 1,\ x^6 - 1\}$, so $\dim V = 3$.

steps.title: Work with coefficient vectors
steps.body: Every $p \in \mathcal{P}_6$ is $p(x) = a_0 + a_1x + a_2x^2 + \dots + a_6x^6$, so $p \leftrightarrow (a_0, \dots, a_6) \in \mathbb{R}^7$ and $\dim \mathcal{P}_6 = 7$. Both conditions defining $V$ are homogeneous linear equations in these 7 coefficients.

steps.title: Translate the evenness condition
steps.body: $p(x) - p(-x) = 2\,(a_1x + a_3x^3 + a_5x^5)$. This is the zero polynomial for all $x$ exactly when $a_1 = a_3 = a_5 = 0$, which gives **three** independent conditions. What remains is $p(x) = a_0 + a_2x^2 + a_4x^4 + a_6x^6$, with 4 free coefficients.

steps.title: Add the root condition
steps.body: $p(1) = a_0 + a_2 + a_4 + a_6 = 0$. It involves only the surviving coefficients and does not follow from evenness, so it is a fourth independent condition: $a_0 = -(a_2 + a_4 + a_6)$.

steps.title: Write down a basis
steps.body: Substituting, $p(x) = a_2(x^2 - 1) + a_4(x^4 - 1) + a_6(x^6 - 1)$ with $a_2, a_4, a_6$ free. The three polynomials $x^2 - 1,\ x^4 - 1,\ x^6 - 1$ span $V$ and are linearly independent (their leading degrees $2, 4, 6$ are distinct). Hence $\dim V = 3$, which matches rank–nullity: $7 - 4 = 3$.

solution.teaching:
The **dimension** of a vector space is the number of vectors in any basis, informally the number of independent "knobs" needed to describe every element. For polynomial spaces the knobs are the coefficients: $\mathcal{P}_n$ has basis $1, x, \dots, x^n$, so $\dim \mathcal{P}_n = n + 1$.

When a subspace is carved out by **homogeneous linear conditions** on the coefficients, each *independent* condition removes exactly one knob. This is rank–nullity in disguise: identify $p$ with its coefficient vector in $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$. The subspace is then the null space of the constraint matrix, so its dimension is $(n + 1) - \text{rank}$.

The real skill is translating each condition correctly. "Even" ($p(-x) = p(x)$ for all $x$) is not one condition but one per odd power, three in this question ($a_1 = a_3 = a_5 = 0$). "Vanishes at $1$" is one more. With 7 coefficients and 4 independent conditions, $\dim V = 3$. You can write a basis down directly by solving for one coefficient in terms of the free ones.
solution.shortcut: Count free coefficients: $7$ coefficients $-\ 3$ (odd powers forced to zero) $-\ 1$ (the equation $p(1) = 0$) $= 3$.
solution.commonTrap: Answering $4$ (forgetting $p(1) = 0$), $6$ (using only $p(1) = 0$, i.e. $7 - 1$), or $5$ (counting "even" as a single condition). Evenness forces *each* odd-power coefficient to be zero, so it contributes three conditions.

answerVerification.checkCode:
import sympy as sp
x = sp.symbols('x'); a = sp.symbols('a0:7')
p = sum(a[k]*x**k for k in range(7))
eqs = sp.Poly(sp.expand(p - p.subs(x, -x)), x).coeffs() + [p.subs(x, 1)]
M = sp.Matrix([[sp.diff(e, ak) for ak in a] for e in eqs])
print(7 - M.rank())

difficultyRationale: Platform-estimated: EASY — one concept (matrix product and trace, with the cyclic property tr(BA) = tr(AB) as an optional shortcut) and a few multiplications; about 1 minute.
concept: Matrix multiplication of non-square matrices and the cyclic property of the trace.
stem:
Let

$$
A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -1 & 0 \\ 1 & 3 & -2 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad B = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 4 \\ 0 & -2 \\ 5 & 1 \end{bmatrix}.
$$

The trace of the $3 \times 3$ matrix $BA$ is ________.

solution.quick: $\operatorname{tr}(BA) = \operatorname{tr}(AB)$, and $AB$ is only $2 \times 2$. Its diagonal entries are $(AB)_{11} = 2$ and $(AB)_{22} = 4 - 6 - 2 = -4$, so the trace is $2 + (-4) = -2$.

steps.title: Check the shapes
steps.body: $A$ is $2 \times 3$ and $B$ is $3 \times 2$, so $BA$ is $3 \times 3$ and $AB$ is $2 \times 2$. Both are square, and $\operatorname{tr}(BA) = \operatorname{tr}(AB)$ because both equal $\sum_{i}\sum_{k} a_{ik}b_{ki}$.

steps.title: Direct check with $BA$
steps.body:
$$
BA = \begin{bmatrix} 1\cdot2 + 4\cdot1 & 1\cdot(-1) + 4\cdot3 & 1\cdot0 + 4\cdot(-2) \\ 0\cdot2 + (-2)\cdot1 & 0\cdot(-1) + (-2)\cdot3 & 0\cdot0 + (-2)(-2) \\ 5\cdot2 + 1\cdot1 & 5\cdot(-1) + 1\cdot3 & 5\cdot0 + 1\cdot(-2) \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 6 & 11 & -8 \\ -2 & -6 & 4 \\ 11 & -2 & -2 \end{bmatrix}
$$

$\operatorname{tr}(BA) = 6 + (-6) + (-2) = -2$, which agrees with Step 2.

solution.teaching:
The **trace** of a square matrix is the sum of its diagonal entries. It is defined only for square matrices, but $AB$ and $BA$ are both square whenever $A$ is $m \times n$ and $B$ is $n \times m$, even though their sizes differ ($m \times m$ versus $n \times n$).

Writing out the diagonal gives the key identity:

$$
\operatorname{tr}(AB) = \sum_{i=1}^{m} \sum_{k=1}^{n} a_{ik} b_{ki} = \sum_{k=1}^{n} \sum_{i=1}^{m} b_{ki} a_{ik} = \operatorname{tr}(BA).
$$

Both traces are the same double sum of products $a_{ik}b_{ki}$; only the order of summation differs. This **cyclic property** extends to longer products, $\operatorname{tr}(ABC) = \operatorname{tr}(BCA) = \operatorname{tr}(CAB)$, but not to arbitrary reorderings.

Here the requested product $BA$ is $3 \times 3$, while $AB$ is only $2 \times 2$. Computing just the two diagonal entries of $AB$ gives $-2$ with the least arithmetic, and the full $BA$ confirms it.
solution.shortcut: $\operatorname{tr}(BA) = \sum_{i,k} a_{ik}b_{ki}$: multiply $A$ entrywise with $B^{\top} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 5 \\ 4 & -2 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$ and add all six products: $2 + 0 + 0 + 4 - 6 - 2 = -2$.
solution.commonTrap: Assuming that $\operatorname{tr}(BA)$ and $\operatorname{tr}(AB)$ must differ because the matrices have different sizes, or making a sign slip in $(AB)_{22} = 4 - 6 - 2$ (for example, taking $(-2) \cdot 1$ as $+2$ and getting $0$ or $2$).

answerVerification.checkCode:
import numpy as np
A = np.array([[2, -1, 0], [1, 3, -2]])
B = np.array([[1, 4], [0, -2], [5, 1]])
print(np.trace(B @ A), np.trace(A @ B))

difficultyRationale: Platform-estimated: EASY — every statement is a one-line consequence of a single idea (rank compared with the number of rows and columns, plus rank–nullity); about 1–1.5 minutes in total.
concept: Existence and uniqueness of solutions of Ax = b from the rank of A (full row rank, rank–nullity).
stem:
A system of $4$ linear equations in $6$ unknowns is written as $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$, where $A$ is a $4 \times 6$ real matrix with $\operatorname{rank}(A) = 4$, $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^6$ and $\mathbf{b} \in \mathbb{R}^4$.

Which of the following statements is/are correct?

options.label: A
options.text: For every $\mathbf{b} \in \mathbb{R}^4$, the system $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ has at least one solution.

options.label: B
options.text: There exists some $\mathbf{b} \in \mathbb{R}^4$ for which $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ has exactly one solution.

options.label: C
options.text: The set of all solutions of $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}$ is a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^6$ of dimension $2$.

options.label: D
options.text: If $\mathbf{b} \ne \mathbf{0}$ and $\mathbf{x}_1, \mathbf{x}_2$ are solutions of $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$, then $\mathbf{x}_1 + \mathbf{x}_2$ is also a solution of $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$.

solution.quick: Rank $4$ equals the number of rows, so the columns span $\mathbb{R}^4$ and every system is consistent (A true). Nullity $= 6 - 4 = 2$, so the homogeneous solution set is a 2-dimensional subspace (C true), and every consistent system has infinitely many solutions (B false). $A(\mathbf{x}_1 + \mathbf{x}_2) = 2\mathbf{b} \ne \mathbf{b}$ (D false).

steps.title: Existence: the column space
steps.body: $A\mathbf{x}$ is a linear combination of the columns of $A$, so $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ is solvable exactly when $\mathbf{b}$ lies in the column space. $\operatorname{rank}(A) = 4$ means the column space is a 4-dimensional subspace of $\mathbb{R}^4$, i.e. all of $\mathbb{R}^4$. Equivalently, $\operatorname{rank}[A \mid \mathbf{b}] \le 4 = \operatorname{rank}(A)$ for every $\mathbf{b}$. **(A) is true.**

steps.title: The null space: rank–nullity
steps.body: The solution set of $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}$ is the null space $N(A)$, which is always a subspace. By rank–nullity, $\dim N(A) = n - \operatorname{rank}(A) = 6 - 4 = 2$. **(C) is true.**

steps.title: Uniqueness never holds
steps.body: If $\mathbf{x}_p$ solves $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$, then the complete solution set is $\{\mathbf{x}_p + \mathbf{n} : \mathbf{n} \in N(A)\}$. Since $N(A)$ is 2-dimensional, it contains infinitely many vectors, so every consistent system (and by Step 1 every system) has infinitely many solutions, forming a 2-parameter family. No $\mathbf{b}$ gives exactly one solution. **(B) is false.**

steps.title: Sums of solutions of a non-homogeneous system
steps.body: $A(\mathbf{x}_1 + \mathbf{x}_2) = A\mathbf{x}_1 + A\mathbf{x}_2 = \mathbf{b} + \mathbf{b} = 2\mathbf{b}$, and $2\mathbf{b} \ne \mathbf{b}$ because $\mathbf{b} \ne \mathbf{0}$. The solution set of $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ is a translate of $N(A)$ (an affine set), not a subspace. It is the *difference* $\mathbf{x}_1 - \mathbf{x}_2$ that lies in $N(A)$. **(D) is false.**

solution.teaching:
For an $m \times n$ matrix $A$ of rank $r$, two facts control the system $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$.

**Existence** depends on the column space. $A\mathbf{x}$ is a combination of the columns, so a solution exists exactly when $\mathbf{b}$ lies in the column space, whose dimension is $r$. If $r = m$ (full row rank), the column space is all of $\mathbb{R}^m$ and every $\mathbf{b}$ works.

**Uniqueness** depends on the null space. If $\mathbf{x}_p$ is one solution, every solution has the form $\mathbf{x}_p + \mathbf{n}$ with $A\mathbf{n} = \mathbf{0}$. By rank–nullity, $\dim N(A) = n - r$, so uniqueness needs $n - r = 0$ (full column rank).

Here $m = 4$, $n = 6$ and $r = 4$: the matrix has full row rank but not full column rank. Every system is therefore consistent, with a 2-parameter family of solutions. The homogeneous solution set is a subspace. For $\mathbf{b} \ne \mathbf{0}$, the solution set is a shifted copy of that subspace, which is not closed under addition.

optionAnalysis.label: A
optionAnalysis.explanation: Correct. Rank $4$ equals the number of equations, so the column space is all of $\mathbb{R}^4$ and every right-hand side is reachable.

optionAnalysis.label: B
optionAnalysis.explanation: Incorrect. Uniqueness would need $N(A) = \{\mathbf{0}\}$, i.e. rank $6$. With nullity $2$, every consistent system has infinitely many solutions. This option confuses full *row* rank (existence) with full *column* rank (uniqueness).

optionAnalysis.label: C
optionAnalysis.explanation: Correct. $N(A)$ is always a subspace, and rank–nullity gives $\dim N(A) = 6 - 4 = 2$.

optionAnalysis.label: D
optionAnalysis.explanation: Incorrect. $A(\mathbf{x}_1 + \mathbf{x}_2) = 2\mathbf{b} \ne \mathbf{b}$. Solutions of a non-homogeneous system form an affine set; only $\mathbf{x}_1 - \mathbf{x}_2$ is guaranteed to lie in $N(A)$.

solution.shortcut: For an $m \times n$ matrix of rank $r$: $r = m$ means the system is always consistent, and $r = n$ means it has at most one solution. Here $r = m = 4 < n = 6$, so every system is consistent and none has a unique solution. The number of free parameters is $n - r = 2$.
solution.commonTrap: Mixing up the two rank conditions: full row rank guarantees *existence*, while full column rank guarantees *uniqueness*. A second trap is treating the solution set of $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ with $\mathbf{b} \ne \mathbf{0}$ as if it were closed under addition (option D).

answerVerification.independentAnswer: A, C (rank 4, nullity 2; random b always consistent; second solution differs; x1+x2 fails)
answerVerification.checkCode:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
A = rng.integers(-5, 6, size=(4, 6)).astype(float)
r = np.linalg.matrix_rank(A); print('rank', r, 'nullity', 6 - r)
b = rng.normal(size=4)
x1 = np.linalg.lstsq(A, b, rcond=None)[0]
print('A consistent for random b:', np.allclose(A @ x1, b))
N = np.linalg.svd(A)[2][r:]            # basis of null space
x2 = x1 + N.T @ rng.normal(size=6 - r)  # a second, different solution
print('B unique?', np.allclose(x1, x2), np.allclose(A @ x2, b))
print('D x1+x2 solves Ax=b?', np.allclose(A @ (x1 + x2), b))
print('Answer: A, C')

difficultyRationale: Platform-estimated: EASY — one concept (eigenvalues of a polynomial in a triangular matrix are the polynomial applied to the diagonal entries) with three one-line evaluations; about 1 minute.
concept: Eigenvalues of a triangular matrix and of a polynomial in a matrix: λ is an eigenvalue of A implies f(λ) is an eigenvalue of f(A).
stem:
Let

$$
A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 5 & -1 \\ 0 & -1 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 3 \end{bmatrix}
$$

and let $B = A^2 - 2A$. The eigenvalues of $B$, listed with algebraic multiplicity, are

solution.quick: $A$ is upper triangular, so its eigenvalues are $2, -1, 3$. The eigenvalues of $B = f(A)$ with $f(\lambda) = \lambda^2 - 2\lambda$ are $f(2) = 0$, $f(-1) = 3$ and $f(3) = 3$.

steps.title: Eigenvalues of $A$
steps.body: $A$ is upper triangular, so $\det(A - \lambda I) = (2 - \lambda)(-1 - \lambda)(3 - \lambda)$ and the eigenvalues are the diagonal entries $2, -1, 3$.

steps.title: Eigenvalues of a polynomial in $A$
steps.body: If $A\mathbf{v} = \lambda\mathbf{v}$, then $A^2\mathbf{v} = \lambda^2\mathbf{v}$, so $B\mathbf{v} = (A^2 - 2A)\mathbf{v} = (\lambda^2 - 2\lambda)\mathbf{v}$. The eigenvalues of $B$ are therefore $f(\lambda) = \lambda^2 - 2\lambda = \lambda(\lambda - 2)$ evaluated at $2, -1, 3$.

steps.title: Cross-check
steps.body: $B$ is upper triangular (sums and products of upper-triangular matrices stay upper triangular), with diagonal entries $\lambda_i^2 - 2\lambda_i = (0, 3, 3)$. So $\operatorname{tr}(B) = 6 = 0 + 3 + 3$, and $\det(B) = 0$, which is consistent with $B = A(A - 2I)$ and the singular factor $A - 2I$.

solution.teaching:
An **eigenvector** $\mathbf{v} \ne \mathbf{0}$ of $A$ satisfies $A\mathbf{v} = \lambda\mathbf{v}$: $A$ only stretches it by the factor $\lambda$. Applying $A$ again stretches it again, so $A^2\mathbf{v} = \lambda^2\mathbf{v}$, and in general $A^k\mathbf{v} = \lambda^k\mathbf{v}$. Since a matrix polynomial is built from powers, sums and scalar multiples, every polynomial $f$ satisfies

$$
f(A)\mathbf{v} = f(\lambda)\mathbf{v}.
$$

In fact the eigenvalues of $f(A)$, counted with algebraic multiplicity, are exactly $f(\lambda_1), \dots, f(\lambda_n)$.

For a triangular matrix the eigenvalues are simply the diagonal entries, because $A - \lambda I$ is also triangular and its determinant is the product of its diagonal entries. Put the two facts together: read $2, -1, 3$ off the diagonal and apply $f(\lambda) = \lambda^2 - 2\lambda$. Two different eigenvalues of $A$ can map to the same eigenvalue of $f(A)$, which is why $3$ appears twice.

optionAnalysis.label: A
optionAnalysis.explanation: Incorrect. These are $\lambda^2$ for $\lambda = 2, -1, 3$, the eigenvalues of $A^2$ alone. The $-2A$ term has been dropped.

optionAnalysis.label: B
optionAnalysis.explanation: Correct. $f(\lambda) = \lambda^2 - 2\lambda$ gives $f(2) = 0$, $f(-1) = 3$ and $f(3) = 3$.

optionAnalysis.label: C
optionAnalysis.explanation: Incorrect. These are $\lambda^2 - 2$, the eigenvalues of $A^2 - 2I$. This confuses $2A$ with $2I$.

optionAnalysis.label: D
optionAnalysis.explanation: Incorrect. This comes from a sign slip at $\lambda = -1$: the value $-2\lambda = +2$ was taken as $-2$, giving $1 - 2 = -1$ instead of $1 + 2 = 3$.

solution.shortcut: For a triangular $A$, $f(A)$ is triangular with diagonal entries $f(a_{ii})$. Apply $f$ to the diagonal and read off the answer.
solution.commonTrap: Evaluating $-2\lambda$ at $\lambda = -1$ as $-2$ instead of $+2$ (giving option D), or computing the eigenvalues of $A^2$ and forgetting the $-2A$ term (option A).

import numpy as np
A = np.array([[2, 5, -1], [0, -1, 4], [0, 0, 3]], dtype=float)
B = A @ A - 2 * A
print([float(x) for x in sorted(np.round(np.linalg.eigvals(B).real, 10))])

difficultyRationale: Platform-estimated: MODERATE — two linked ideas (effect of elementary row operations on det, then the scalar-multiple, inverse, transpose and product rules) applied in three short steps; about 2 minutes.
concept: Determinant under elementary row operations, and the rules det(kM) = kⁿ det M, det(M⁻¹) = 1/det M, det(Mᵀ) = det M, det(XY) = det X · det Y.
stem:
Let $A$ and $B$ be real $3 \times 3$ matrices with $\det(A) = 2$ and $\det(B) = -5$. A matrix $C$ is obtained from $A$ in two steps: first, the first and third rows of $A$ are interchanged; then $4$ times the (new) first row is added to the second row.

The value of $\det\!\left(3\,C^{-1}B^{\top}\right)$ is

solution.quick: The row interchange flips the sign and the row addition changes nothing, so $\det(C) = -2$. Then $\det(3C^{-1}B^{\top}) = 3^3 \cdot \frac{1}{-2} \cdot (-5) = 27 \times 2.5 = 67.5$.

steps.title: Effect of the row operations
steps.body:
- Interchanging two rows multiplies the determinant by $-1$, which gives $-2$.
- Adding a multiple of one row to another row leaves the determinant unchanged, so it stays $-2$.

Hence $\det(C) = -\det(A) = -2$. In particular $C$ is invertible, so $C^{-1}$ exists.

steps.title: Rules needed for the product
steps.body: For $n \times n$ matrices: $\det(kM) = k^n\det(M)$, $\det(XY) = \det(X)\det(Y)$, $\det(M^{-1}) = \dfrac{1}{\det(M)}$ and $\det(M^{\top}) = \det(M)$. Here $n = 3$.

steps.title: Substitute
steps.body:
$$
\det\!\left(3\,C^{-1}B^{\top}\right) = 3^3 \cdot \det(C^{-1}) \cdot \det(B^{\top}) = 27 \cdot \frac{1}{-2} \cdot (-5) = \frac{135}{2} = 67.5.
$$

solution.teaching:
Think of the determinant of a $3 \times 3$ matrix as the **signed volume** of the box spanned by its rows. Each elementary row operation changes this volume in a predictable way:

- **Interchanging two rows** reverses orientation, so the determinant changes sign.
- **Adding a multiple of one row to another** is a shear: it tilts the box without changing its volume, so the determinant is unchanged.
- **Multiplying one row by $k$** stretches one edge, so the determinant is multiplied by $k$.

Multiplying the *whole* matrix by $k$ scales all $n$ rows, so $\det(kM) = k^n\det(M)$. The product rule $\det(XY) = \det(X)\det(Y)$ gives $\det(M^{-1}) = 1/\det(M)$ (because $MM^{-1} = I$), and transposing does not change the determinant.

In this question the swap flips the sign of $\det(A) = 2$, the row addition does nothing, and the remaining factors follow from the rules: $27 \times \frac{1}{-2} \times (-5) = 67.5$.

optionAnalysis.label: A
optionAnalysis.explanation: Incorrect. This treats "add $4 \times$ row 1 to row 2" as if it multiplied the determinant by $4$, so $\det(C) = -8$ and $27 \cdot \frac{1}{-8} \cdot (-5) = 16.875$. Adding a multiple of another row does not change the determinant.

optionAnalysis.label: B
optionAnalysis.explanation: Incorrect. This ignores the sign change from the row interchange, taking $\det(C) = 2$: $27 \cdot \frac{1}{2} \cdot (-5) = -67.5$.

optionAnalysis.label: C
optionAnalysis.explanation: Correct. $\det(C) = -2$, so $3^3 \cdot \frac{1}{-2} \cdot (-5) = 67.5$.

optionAnalysis.label: D
optionAnalysis.explanation: Incorrect. This uses $\det(3M) = 3\det(M)$ instead of $3^3\det(M)$: $3 \cdot \frac{1}{-2} \cdot (-5) = 7.5$.

solution.commonTrap: Writing $\det(3M) = 3\det(M)$. The scalar multiplies every one of the three rows, so the factor is $3^3 = 27$. Another slip is forgetting to invert $\det(C)$, which gives $27 \cdot (-2) \cdot (-5) = 270$.

import numpy as np
A = np.diag([2.0, 1.0, 1.0]); A[0, 1] = 3; A[2, 0] = 1   # det(A) = 2
B = np.diag([-5.0, 1.0, 1.0]); B[1, 2] = 4              # det(B) = -5
C = A[[2, 1, 0], :].copy()     # swap rows 1 and 3
C[1] = C[1] + 4 * C[0]         # add 4 x (new) row 1 to row 2
print(round(np.linalg.det(A), 6), round(np.linalg.det(B), 6), round(np.linalg.det(C), 6))
print(round(np.linalg.det(3 * np.linalg.inv(C) @ B.T), 6))

difficultyRationale: Platform-estimated: MODERATE — one concept (orthogonal projection onto a subspace) applied in 2–3 routine steps (check orthogonality, two coefficients, residual norm) plus a property check on P; about 2.5 minutes.
concept: Orthogonal projection onto a subspace with an orthogonal basis; residual orthogonality, distance to a subspace, and properties of projection matrices.
stem:
In $\mathbb{R}^4$ with the standard inner product, let $W = \operatorname{span}\{\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}\}$, where

$$
\mathbf{a} = (1,\ 1,\ 0,\ 1)^{\top}, \qquad \mathbf{b} = (1,\ -1,\ 1,\ 0)^{\top},
$$

and let $\mathbf{v} = (3,\ 1,\ 4,\ 2)^{\top}$. Let $P$ be the $4 \times 4$ matrix of the orthogonal projection of $\mathbb{R}^4$ onto $W$.

Which of the following statements is/are correct?

options.label: B
options.text: The distance from $\mathbf{v}$ to the subspace $W$ is $\sqrt{6}$.

options.label: C
options.text: $P$ is an orthogonal matrix, that is, $P^{\top}P = I_4$.

options.label: D
options.text: The vector $(-1,\ 1,\ 2,\ 0)^{\top}$ is orthogonal to every vector in $W$.

solution.quick: $\mathbf{a}^{\top}\mathbf{b} = 0$, so $P\mathbf{v} = \frac{6}{3}\mathbf{a} + \frac{6}{3}\mathbf{b} = (4, 0, 2, 2)^{\top}$ (A). The residual $(-1, 1, 2, 0)^{\top}$ is orthogonal to $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ (D), and its length is $\sqrt{6}$ (B). $P$ has rank $2$, so $P^{\top}P = P \ne I_4$ (C false).

steps.title: Check whether the basis is orthogonal
steps.body:
$\mathbf{a}^{\top}\mathbf{b} = 1 - 1 + 0 + 0 = 0$. Because the basis is orthogonal, the projection is the sum of the one-dimensional projections:

$$
P\mathbf{v} = \frac{\mathbf{a}^{\top}\mathbf{v}}{\mathbf{a}^{\top}\mathbf{a}}\,\mathbf{a} + \frac{\mathbf{b}^{\top}\mathbf{v}}{\mathbf{b}^{\top}\mathbf{b}}\,\mathbf{b}.
$$

steps.title: Compute the projection
steps.body:
$\mathbf{a}^{\top}\mathbf{v} = 3 + 1 + 0 + 2 = 6$ and $\mathbf{a}^{\top}\mathbf{a} = 3$, so the coefficient is $2$.

$\mathbf{b}^{\top}\mathbf{v} = 3 - 1 + 4 + 0 = 6$ and $\mathbf{b}^{\top}\mathbf{b} = 3$, so the coefficient is $2$.

$P\mathbf{v} = 2\mathbf{a} + 2\mathbf{b} = (2, 2, 0, 2) + (2, -2, 2, 0) = (4, 0, 2, 2)^{\top}$. **(A) is true.**

steps.title: Residual and distance
steps.body:
$\mathbf{r} = \mathbf{v} - P\mathbf{v} = (-1, 1, 2, 0)^{\top}$.

$\mathbf{r}^{\top}\mathbf{a} = -1 + 1 + 0 + 0 = 0$ and $\mathbf{r}^{\top}\mathbf{b} = -1 - 1 + 2 + 0 = 0$, so $\mathbf{r}$ is orthogonal to every $\alpha\mathbf{a} + \beta\mathbf{b} \in W$. **(D) is true.**

The distance from $\mathbf{v}$ to $W$ is $\lVert\mathbf{r}\rVert = \sqrt{1 + 1 + 4 + 0} = \sqrt{6} \approx 2.449$. **(B) is true.** Pythagoras check: $\lVert\mathbf{v}\rVert^2 = 30 = \lVert P\mathbf{v}\rVert^2 + \lVert\mathbf{r}\rVert^2 = 24 + 6$.

steps.title: Is $P$ an orthogonal matrix?
steps.body: An orthogonal projection matrix is symmetric and idempotent, so $P^{\top}P = P^2 = P$. Since $\operatorname{rank}(P) = \dim W = 2 < 4$, $P \ne I_4$. For example, $P\mathbf{r} = \mathbf{0}$ although $\mathbf{r} \ne \mathbf{0}$, so $P$ is not even invertible. **(C) is false.**

solution.teaching:
The **orthogonal projection** of $\mathbf{v}$ onto a subspace $W$ is the unique vector $\hat{\mathbf{v}} \in W$ whose error $\mathbf{v} - \hat{\mathbf{v}}$ is orthogonal to every vector of $W$. It is also the point of $W$ closest to $\mathbf{v}$, so $\lVert\mathbf{v} - \hat{\mathbf{v}}\rVert$ is the distance from $\mathbf{v}$ to $W$.

If $W$ has an **orthogonal** basis $\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}$, the projection splits into independent one-dimensional pieces, $\hat{\mathbf{v}} = \frac{\mathbf{a}^{\top}\mathbf{v}}{\mathbf{a}^{\top}\mathbf{a}}\mathbf{a} + \frac{\mathbf{b}^{\top}\mathbf{v}}{\mathbf{b}^{\top}\mathbf{b}}\mathbf{b}$. For a general basis (the columns of $M$) you need $P = M(M^{\top}M)^{-1}M^{\top}$. With an orthogonal basis, $M^{\top}M$ is diagonal and this collapses to the simple sum.

Every orthogonal projection matrix is symmetric and idempotent. Its eigenvalues are only $0$ and $1$, and its trace equals its rank, $\dim W$. An orthogonal matrix ($Q^{\top}Q = I$) is quite different: it preserves lengths and is always invertible.

optionAnalysis.label: A
optionAnalysis.explanation: Correct. Since $\mathbf{a} \perp \mathbf{b}$, $P\mathbf{v} = 2\mathbf{a} + 2\mathbf{b} = (4, 0, 2, 2)^{\top}$.

optionAnalysis.label: B
optionAnalysis.explanation: Correct. The residual $(-1, 1, 2, 0)^{\top}$ has squared length $6$, so the distance is $\sqrt{6}$. Reporting $6$ would give the squared distance instead.

optionAnalysis.label: C
optionAnalysis.explanation: Incorrect. This confuses "orthogonal projection" with "orthogonal matrix". Here $P^{\top}P = P$, which has rank $2$ and cannot equal $I_4$; $P$ is singular.

optionAnalysis.label: D
optionAnalysis.explanation: Correct. Its dot products with $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ are both $0$, so it is orthogonal to every combination $\alpha\mathbf{a} + \beta\mathbf{b}$. It is exactly the residual $\mathbf{v} - P\mathbf{v}$.

solution.shortcut: Because $\mathbf{a} \perp \mathbf{b}$, project onto each vector separately and add. Then the squared distance is $\lVert\mathbf{v}\rVert^2 - \lVert P\mathbf{v}\rVert^2 = 30 - 24 = 6$.
solution.commonTrap: Adding one-dimensional projections without first checking that the basis vectors are orthogonal. It works here only because $\mathbf{a}^{\top}\mathbf{b} = 0$. Other slips are reporting the squared distance $6$ as the distance, and confusing an orthogonal *projection* matrix with an orthogonal matrix.

answerVerification.independentAnswer: A, B, D (Pv = (4,0,2,2), dist = sqrt(6) = 2.449, P^T P != I, residual orthogonal to a and b)
answerVerification.checkCode:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([1, 1, 0, 1.]); b = np.array([1, -1, 1, 0.]); v = np.array([3, 1, 4, 2.])
M = np.column_stack([a, b])
P = M @ np.linalg.inv(M.T @ M) @ M.T
r = v - P @ v
print('a.b =', a @ b)
print('A: Pv =', np.round(P @ v, 10))
print('B: dist =', np.linalg.norm(r), 'sqrt6 =', np.sqrt(6))
print('C: P^T P = I ?', np.allclose(P.T @ P, np.eye(4)), 'trace', round(np.trace(P), 10))
print('D: residual =', np.round(r, 10), 'dots', round(r @ a, 10), round(r @ b, 10))
print('Answer: A, B, D')

difficultyRationale: Platform-estimated: EASY — a single concept (the three-part subspace test), with each wrong option dismissed by one quick counterexample; about 1 minute.
concept: Subspace test (zero vector, closure under addition and scalar multiplication) applied to subsets of the space of 2×2 matrices.
stem:
Let $M_2(\mathbb{R})$ be the vector space of all $2 \times 2$ real matrices under the usual matrix addition and multiplication by real scalars. Write a matrix as

$$
X = \begin{bmatrix} x_{11} & x_{12} \\ x_{21} & x_{22} \end{bmatrix}.
$$

Which one of the following subsets of $M_2(\mathbb{R})$ is a subspace of $M_2(\mathbb{R})$?

options.label: A
options.text: The set of all invertible $2 \times 2$ real matrices

options.label: B
options.text: The set of all $2 \times 2$ matrices whose four entries are all integers

options.label: C
options.text: The set of all $2 \times 2$ real matrices $X$ with $\det(X) = 0$

options.label: D
options.text: The set of all $2 \times 2$ real matrices $X$ with $x_{11} + x_{22} = x_{12}$

solution.quick: Only (D) is defined by a homogeneous linear equation in the entries ($x_{11} + x_{22} - x_{12} = 0$), so it is closed under linear combinations. (A) misses the zero matrix, (B) fails under scaling by $\tfrac12$, and (C) fails under addition ($\operatorname{diag}(1,0) + \operatorname{diag}(0,1) = I$).

steps.title: The subspace test
steps.body: A subset $S$ is a subspace when (i) the zero matrix $O \in S$, (ii) $X, Y \in S \Rightarrow X + Y \in S$, and (iii) $X \in S,\ c \in \mathbb{R} \Rightarrow cX \in S$. One counterexample to any of these is enough to rule a set out.

steps.title: Options (A) and (B)
steps.body:
(A): $O$ is not invertible, so (i) fails. Closure under addition fails as well: $I + (-I) = O$.

(B): $O$ is in the set and sums of integer matrices are integer matrices, but $\tfrac12 I = \begin{bmatrix} 0.5 & 0 \\ 0 & 0.5 \end{bmatrix}$ has non-integer entries, so (iii) fails for the real scalar $c = \tfrac12$.

steps.title: Option (C)
steps.body: $O$ is singular, and $\det(cX) = c^2\det(X) = 0$, so (i) and (iii) hold. But $\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = I$ with $\det(I) = 1 \ne 0$, so (ii) fails.

steps.title: Option (D)
steps.body:
The defining condition is $x_{11} + x_{22} - x_{12} = 0$. If $X$ and $Y$ satisfy it, then for any reals $\alpha, \beta$:

$$
(\alpha x_{11} + \beta y_{11}) + (\alpha x_{22} + \beta y_{22}) - (\alpha x_{12} + \beta y_{12}) = \alpha \cdot 0 + \beta \cdot 0 = 0.
$$

$O$ also satisfies it. So (D) is a subspace; it is the null space of a nonzero linear functional on the 4-dimensional space $M_2(\mathbb{R})$, and so has dimension $3$.

optionAnalysis.label: A
optionAnalysis.explanation: Incorrect. The zero matrix is not invertible, so the set has no zero vector. Also $I + (-I) = O$ leaves the set.

optionAnalysis.label: B
optionAnalysis.explanation: Incorrect. It is closed under addition, but not under multiplication by arbitrary real scalars: $\tfrac12 I$ has entries $0.5$.

optionAnalysis.label: C
optionAnalysis.explanation: Incorrect. It contains $O$ and is closed under scaling, but not under addition: $\operatorname{diag}(1, 0) + \operatorname{diag}(0, 1) = I$, which is invertible.

optionAnalysis.label: D
optionAnalysis.explanation: Correct. $x_{11} + x_{22} - x_{12} = 0$ is a homogeneous linear condition, so the set contains $O$ and is closed under all linear combinations. It is a 3-dimensional subspace.

solution.shortcut: Look for the option defined by a homogeneous *linear* equation in the entries. Conditions involving determinants, invertibility or integrality are almost never subspaces.
solution.commonTrap: Choosing (C) because the zero matrix is singular and scalar multiples of singular matrices stay singular. Containing $O$ and being closed under scaling is not enough: closure under addition fails.

answerVerification.independentAnswer: D (counterexamples confirm A, B, C fail; D closed under 1000 random linear combinations)
answerVerification.checkCode:
import numpy as np
from fractions import Fraction as F
# (A) invertible: zero matrix missing
print('A zero invertible?', np.linalg.det(np.zeros((2, 2))) != 0)
# (B) integer entries: 0.5 * I not integer
print('B 0.5*I integer?', np.all(np.mod(0.5 * np.eye(2), 1) == 0))
# (C) det 0: diag(1,0)+diag(0,1)=I
print('C sum det =', np.linalg.det(np.diag([1., 0]) + np.diag([0., 1])))
# (D) a11 + a22 - a12 = 0 is a linear functional -> kernel is a subspace
f = lambda X: X[0][0] + X[1][1] - X[0][1]
rng = np.random.default_rng(1); ok = True
for _ in range(1000):
    X = rng.normal(size=(2, 2)); X[0, 1] = X[0, 0] + X[1, 1]
    Y = rng.normal(size=(2, 2)); Y[0, 1] = Y[0, 0] + Y[1, 1]
    c, d = rng.normal(size=2)
    ok &= abs(f(c * X + d * Y)) < 1e-9
print('D closed under linear combos:', ok, '; zero in D:', f(np.zeros((2, 2))) == 0)
print('Answer: D')

difficultyRationale: Platform-estimated: EASY — one concept (the projection I − uuᵀ/uᵀu onto the orthogonal complement of a line), evaluated with one dot product and one vector subtraction; about 1 minute.
concept: Projection matrix onto the orthogonal complement of a line: P = I − uuᵀ/(uᵀu) removes the component along u.
stem:
A feature-cleaning step removes from every vector in $\mathbb{R}^3$ its component along the direction $\mathbf{u} = (2,\ -1,\ 2)^{\top}$ by applying the matrix

$$
P = I_3 - \frac{\mathbf{u}\mathbf{u}^{\top}}{\mathbf{u}^{\top}\mathbf{u}}.
$$

For $\mathbf{w} = (1,\ 1,\ 1)^{\top}$, the vector $P\mathbf{w}$ is

steps.title: Recognise the matrix
steps.body: $\dfrac{\mathbf{u}\mathbf{u}^{\top}}{\mathbf{u}^{\top}\mathbf{u}}$ is the orthogonal projection onto the line through $\mathbf{u}$. So $P = I - \dfrac{\mathbf{u}\mathbf{u}^{\top}}{\mathbf{u}^{\top}\mathbf{u}}$ is the orthogonal projection onto the plane $\mathbf{u}^{\perp}$. It satisfies $P^{\top} = P$, $P^2 = P$ and $P\mathbf{u} = \mathbf{0}$.

steps.title: Apply it without forming the $3 \times 3$ matrix
steps.body:
$P\mathbf{w} = \mathbf{w} - \dfrac{\mathbf{u}^{\top}\mathbf{w}}{\mathbf{u}^{\top}\mathbf{u}}\,\mathbf{u}$, with

$\mathbf{u}^{\top}\mathbf{u} = 4 + 1 + 4 = 9$ and $\mathbf{u}^{\top}\mathbf{w} = 2 - 1 + 2 = 3$,

so the coefficient is $\dfrac{3}{9} = \dfrac13$.

steps.title: Subtract
steps.body: $P\mathbf{w} = (1, 1, 1) - \tfrac13(2, -1, 2) = \left(1 - \tfrac23,\ 1 + \tfrac13,\ 1 - \tfrac23\right) = \left(\tfrac13,\ \tfrac43,\ \tfrac13\right)^{\top}$.

steps.title: Verify
steps.body: $\mathbf{u}^{\top}(P\mathbf{w}) = \tfrac23 - \tfrac43 + \tfrac23 = 0$, so the component along $\mathbf{u}$ has indeed been removed. Also $P\mathbf{w} + \tfrac13\mathbf{u} = \mathbf{w}$, as expected.

solution.teaching:
For a nonzero vector $\mathbf{u}$, the matrix $\frac{\mathbf{u}\mathbf{u}^{\top}}{\mathbf{u}^{\top}\mathbf{u}}$ sends any $\mathbf{w}$ to $\frac{\mathbf{u}^{\top}\mathbf{w}}{\mathbf{u}^{\top}\mathbf{u}}\,\mathbf{u}$, the component of $\mathbf{w}$ along $\mathbf{u}$. It is the orthogonal projection onto the line through $\mathbf{u}$.

Subtracting it from the identity keeps everything *except* that component, so $P = I - \frac{\mathbf{u}\mathbf{u}^{\top}}{\mathbf{u}^{\top}\mathbf{u}}$ projects orthogonally onto the plane of vectors perpendicular to $\mathbf{u}$. Like every orthogonal projection matrix it is symmetric and idempotent; here $P\mathbf{u} = \mathbf{0}$ and $\operatorname{rank}(P) = 2$.

Dividing by $\mathbf{u}^{\top}\mathbf{u} = \lVert\mathbf{u}\rVert^2$, not by $\lVert\mathbf{u}\rVert$, is what makes the formula valid for a $\mathbf{u}$ that is not a unit vector. The related matrix $I - 2\frac{\mathbf{u}\mathbf{u}^{\top}}{\mathbf{u}^{\top}\mathbf{u}}$ *reflects* across the plane instead; it is orthogonal but not idempotent. In data pipelines, this "remove one direction" projection strips a nuisance direction (such as a trend or bias direction) from feature vectors.

optionAnalysis.label: A
optionAnalysis.explanation: Correct. $\mathbf{w} - \tfrac13\mathbf{u} = \left(\tfrac13, \tfrac43, \tfrac13\right)$, and its dot product with $\mathbf{u}$ is $0$.

optionAnalysis.label: B
optionAnalysis.explanation: Incorrect. This is $\mathbf{w} + \tfrac13\mathbf{u}$: the component along $\mathbf{u}$ has been added instead of subtracted. Its dot product with $\mathbf{u}$ is $6 \ne 0$.

optionAnalysis.label: C
optionAnalysis.explanation: Incorrect. This is $\mathbf{w} - \tfrac23\mathbf{u}$, the Householder *reflection* $\left(I - 2\frac{\mathbf{u}\mathbf{u}^{\top}}{\mathbf{u}^{\top}\mathbf{u}}\right)\mathbf{w}$. It flips the $\mathbf{u}$-component rather than removing it; its dot product with $\mathbf{u}$ is $-3$.

optionAnalysis.label: D
optionAnalysis.explanation: Incorrect. This is $\tfrac13\mathbf{u} = \frac{\mathbf{u}\mathbf{u}^{\top}}{\mathbf{u}^{\top}\mathbf{u}}\mathbf{w}$, the component that is *removed*, not what remains.

solution.shortcut: Use $P\mathbf{w} = \mathbf{w} - \frac{\mathbf{u}^{\top}\mathbf{w}}{\mathbf{u}^{\top}\mathbf{u}}\mathbf{u}$, which needs one dot product and no $3 \times 3$ matrix. Then check $\mathbf{u}^{\top}(P\mathbf{w}) = 0$: this test alone eliminates (B), (C) and (D).
solution.commonTrap: Stopping at $\frac{\mathbf{u}\mathbf{u}^{\top}}{\mathbf{u}^{\top}\mathbf{u}}\mathbf{w}$ (option D), or dividing by $\lVert\mathbf{u}\rVert = 3$ instead of $\mathbf{u}^{\top}\mathbf{u} = 9$, which gives $\mathbf{w} - \mathbf{u} = (-1, 2, -1)^{\top}$.
